results.finding: sections, unit counts and unit forms match the spec

All 54 aligned units match their spec controlling ideas in spec order; the three callout entries have no spec paragraph. Closest calls: p42b (draft does not say in words that this is why every copy row has a reconciliation) and p18 (owner of the cross-context view is stated as the OMS's job, not as 'what was missing'); both carry the same idea.
Mirrors the reverse-outline verdict: same controlling ideas, same order, no unmatched or extra body units.

The outliner flagged no unit. Read the densest candidates (Entity-Owner Table ¶1 with its two inline definitions, Facts ¶6 with the master-data parenthesis, Scale Stages ¶2): each serves one idea; the extras are glosses or the example the spec assigns.

Every body unit ties to the supporting claim its section declares (S1 scene and truth patterns, S2 definitions, S3 contexts, S4 table, S5 four ways and stages, S6 failure modes); intro, roadmap and hand-off units are structural.

All eight tables are introduced or followed by a statement of what they show ('as the table shows...', 'Its point is that...', 'Each is a fact without an owner'); quotations are glossed (e.g. 'one writer per entity, enforced by the plumbing'); the five figures carry explanatory captions. Weakest: the four-options table, whose following sentence gives provenance first and reads the Fits/Breaks rows only through 'My rule'.

results.draft_locus: When Ownership Is Not Decided: The Five Truth Patterns ¶1
results.quote: [[where-commerce-platforms-go-wrong]] names five patterns in a family it calls Truth. Each is a fact without an owner.
results.finding: The section opens on a pointer to another chapter and picks up nothing from the preceding text (the ways ownership is assigned, or the suite section's closing quote); only the heading links back, and the cause-effect arrives in the second sentence without the carried-over element.

The other 52 declared boundaries pass: explicit ones (e.g. 'Ruben Alves then put numbers on those six answers', 'Noor's question was not...', 'The same happens with', 'Two design rules follow', 'Two things remain yours even in a suite', 'The new design did not make the copies right by being named') and bold run-in parallels (the four options, the five failure modes, the conclusion's three labels). Passed narrowly, relationship implied rather than worded: Introduction ¶3 (roadmap does not pick up 'the decisions'), Bounded Contexts ¶4 ('For six days, nobody could give the customer a combined view'), Facts ¶5 (writer definition opens without picking up 'never edited').

Every term on the does_not_know list is defined or expanded at first use (system of record, copy, writer, bounded context, event, reconciliation; WMS, ERP, POS, PIM, OMS, PSP, plus SKU, GTIN, EDI, B2B, D2C, 3PL). Incident names (App That Wrote Stock, Double Refund, Price Drift, Store Stock Mirage, Deprecated Endpoint) are glossed in the sentence or cell where they first appear. Not expanded but outside the spec's lists: B2C, API, 'monolith', 'orchestration', 'data warehouse'.
Opens on a concrete puzzling scenario, then the claim and a specific roadmap; none of placeholder, restated question, dictionary opener, dawn of man or book report.

The conclusion is sorted by how settled each point is, cites body evidence by reference only, adds no new subtopic, does not open with 'in conclusion' and ends on a course of action plus hand-off, not a rephrased thesis.

'Write the entity–owner table before buying any hub ... a bought OMS fed by four unreconciled order sources is a fifth copy, and a written table with no reconciliation is a record on trust' is stated by no single section and matches the spec's so_what. The spec's unifying sentence (records, contexts, hub choice and failure modes as one decision seen four ways) is not stated in those words; 'costs nothing' is absent.

'The parcel that opened this chapter, Delivered in the storefront and In picking in the warehouse, was such a case: neither status was stale, each was true of its own object, and what was missing was an owner of the view across them.'

The cold reader predicted all six expected items in the right order (six answers, vocabulary, meanings of 'order', entity-owner table, comparison of ownership choices with vendor documentation, return to Kestrel & Pine's stock). Wrong or missing, not material to the expected answer: placed the Kestrel & Pine return last, so did not foresee the closing failure-modes section; did not foresee the suite section; expected vendor documentation as the only external evidence, whereas the draft also uses Evans, Fowler and the Walmart account.

Cold answer asks which system is the record, then who or what can write the number, and explicitly refuses a hand fix; no 'sync faster'. Slight narrowing: it asks about writers in the shop only, not in each system.
Cold answer: yes, each 'order' is a different object sharing an order number, none is stale, and what is missing is an owner of the view across them (the OMS). Matches expected.

Cold answer fills record, who may write, copies, how copies learn and disagreement found by for consumer price, each specifically (platform price lists; pricing owner with effective dates; storefronts, POS, marketplaces, connector; event on change; hourly per-channel comparison).
